title: Hip osteoarthritis and frailty: getting into a car without a jolt (UK)
meta_title: Hip osteoarthritis and frailty: getting into a car without a jolt
meta_description: Step-by-step tips for getting in and out of a car with painful hip osteoarthritis and frailty, plus aids such as swivel cushions and handy bars.
excerpt: Step-by-step tips for getting in and out of a car with painful hip osteoarthritis and frailty, plus aids such as swivel cushions and handy bars.
direct_answer: Getting into a car can be painful with hip osteoarthritis. Sitting down first and then swinging your legs in together, a higher seat, a swivel cushion or a plastic bag on the seat, and a portable handle can help. An OT can advise on aids.

content:
Car seats are often low, and twisting to get in can jar a painful hip.

This guide covers practical techniques and aids. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

A simple technique

  • Ask for the car to be parked away from the kerb, so the seat is not too low, and with the door fully open.
  • Move the seat back and recline it slightly.
  • Back up to the seat until you feel it behind your legs.
  • Lower yourself onto the seat, keeping hold of something stable.
  • Swing both legs in together, keeping knees together.
  • Reverse the steps to get out.

Aids that may help

  • Swivel cushions or a plastic bag on the seat to make turning easier.
  • Portable handles that fit into the door catch.
  • A firm cushion to raise the seat height.
  • A leg lifter strap.

After a hip replacement

Follow the advice from your surgical team about car travel, as it may differ.

Getting help

An OT can advise on aids and technique. Some driving and mobility centres can assess car adaptations.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is it safe to drive with hip arthritis?

You must be able to control the car safely. Ask your GP if you are unsure.

Where can I get a car handle?

From mobility shops, or ask an OT.
